facts.claim: In the Orthodox marriage service (Orthodox Church in America text, 2022) the service has two parts: a Service of Betrothal, celebrated in the narthex or back of the church, in which the priest blesses the couple with the rings, places them on their right hands and the couple exchange them; then the Service of Crowning in the centre of the church.
facts.conflicts: Text is the Orthodox Church in America edition, not the Antiochian Orthodox Archdiocese; same Byzantine rite but Antiochian practice in Lebanon not confirmed from an Antiochian source.

facts.claim: In the Orthodox Service of Crowning the priest crowns the bridegroom first and then the bride; the service text says the crowns recall those with which the martyrs, or witnesses of Christ, are crowned in heaven, and the priest blesses them three times saying 'O Lord our God, crown them with glory and honor'.

The Orthodox crowning service includes a blessed common cup given to the groom then the bride, after which the priest leads the couple three times around the lectern while the groomsmen behind them hold their crowns.
facts.conflicts: Text says 'groomsmen' hold the crowns; whether sponsors or a koumbaros hold crowns at Lebanese Antiochian weddings is not sourced.

facts.claim: One of the crowning prayers in the Orthodox service asks God to 'exalt them like the cedars of Lebanon, like a luxuriant vine' (Orthodox Church in America text).

Britannica's mahr topic page describes mahr as a marriage custom; its linked article excerpts describe it (India) as the groom's commitment to provide his bride with wealth in her lifetime, and (Yemen) as a usual part of the marriage ceremony. The page gives no Lebanon-specific detail.

Britannica (Lebanon, last updated 2 Nov 2026): Lebanon's two largest religious groups are Shia Muslims and Sunni Muslims; Maronite Christians make up more than one-fifth of the population; other Christian communities, Druze and a small Jewish minority are also present. Lebanon has no official religion.

Britannica describes Lebanon's mountainous terrain as giving it a 'uniquely diverse religious landscape', long home to Maronite Christianity, the Druze faith and the largest Shia community in the Levant.

Encyclopaedic definition: the tulba (also printed tolbe, Arabic طلبة) is a formal request for the bride's hand; it is private, limited to relatives, follows both families agreeing to the couple's decision, and the groom with his family asks the bride and her family, after which the families formally recognise that the couple will marry.
facts.conflicts: Wikipedia (Arab wedding, oldid 1356602611) is flagged 'needs more citations' (June 2025) and is pan-Arab, not Lebanon-specific; use as encyclopaedic definition only, hedged ('across the Levant', 'many families').

facts.claim: Encyclopaedic definition: in the Levant the engagement is called khutubah (خطوبة; khetbah in Saudi usage); engagements in the Arab world usually take place at a simpler party or family dinner without a zaffah, and the couple exchange rings, placing them on each other's right-hand ring finger.
facts.conflicts: Wikipedia (Arab wedding, oldid 1356602611) is flagged 'needs more citations' (June 2025) and is pan-Arab, not Lebanon-specific; use as encyclopaedic definition only, hedged ('across the Levant', 'many families'). Spelling conflict: brief uses 'khutbeh'; source prints 'khutubah'.

facts.claim: Encyclopaedic note: in the Levant, the families reading the Fatiha after the father agrees to the proposal is typically accompanied by Arabic coffee (sharbat is more usual in Egypt). Source frames this under Islamic practice in Egypt, parts of Palestine and Jordan, not Lebanon specifically.
facts.conflicts: Wikipedia (Arab wedding, oldid 1356602611) is flagged 'needs more citations' (June 2025) and is pan-Arab, not Lebanon-specific; use as encyclopaedic definition only, hedged ('across the Levant', 'many families'). Coffee at a Lebanese tulbeh therefore 'often told', not a Lebanon-sourced fact.

facts.claim: Encyclopaedic definition: the Islamic marriage contract is called aqd nikah, aqd qiran, aqd zawaj or katb el-kitab and is the focus of the official ceremony; a sheikh or imam gives a short address, the bride's father or eldest male relative accepts the proposal, the legal documents are completed and filed, and two witnesses sign.
facts.conflicts: Wikipedia (Arab wedding, oldid 1356602611) is flagged 'needs more citations' (June 2025) and is pan-Arab, not Lebanon-specific; use as encyclopaedic definition only, hedged ('across the Levant', 'many families'). Not yet confirmed from Britannica or Encyclopaedia of Islam (not fetched in budget).

facts.claim: Encyclopaedic note: in the Levant the katb al-kitab is usually held at the bride's or groom's family home, or sometimes at the wedding hall, a mosque or a court.
facts.conflicts: Wikipedia (Arab wedding, oldid 1356602611) is flagged 'needs more citations' (June 2025) and is pan-Arab, not Lebanon-specific; use as encyclopaedic definition only, hedged ('across the Levant', 'many families').

facts.claim: Encyclopaedic note: for a Muslim marriage, the only Islamic requirement is the nikah and its announcement; proposal, engagement, henna, reception and walima are cultural additions, and civil registration is usually a legal requirement.
facts.conflicts: Wikipedia (Arab wedding, oldid 1356602611) is flagged 'needs more citations' (June 2025) and is pan-Arab, not Lebanon-specific; use as encyclopaedic definition only, hedged ('across the Levant', 'many families').

facts.claim: Encyclopaedic note citing Lara Deeb, Love Across Difference: Mixed Marriage in Lebanon (Stanford University Press, 2024): about 6 per cent of marriages in Lebanon are interfaith; Lebanese citizens marry under one of 15 personal status laws; some couples who do not wish to change faith opt for a civil marriage abroad. Cultural context only, not legal advice.

Legal statements must come from government sources (batch B / Smartraveller); do not present this as legal guidance.

facts.claim: Henna night (described for Palestine, not Lebanon): historically the groom's family danced through the village to the bride's house where henna was mixed and applied to the couple's hands; today, especially outside Palestine, it resembles a women's celebration with music, food and dancing, with henna drawn on the bride's and guests' palms and feet.
facts.conflicts: Wikipedia (Arab wedding, oldid 1356602611) is flagged 'needs more citations' (June 2025) and is pan-Arab, not Lebanon-specific; use as encyclopaedic definition only, hedged ('across the Levant', 'many families'). Not Lebanon-specific; Lebanese henna night details must be framed as 'often told' or 'across the Levant'.

facts.claim: Melkite Greek Catholic Eparchy of Newton (Fr Philip Raczka): the Eastern Churches' marriage service is called the Mystery of Crowning; it has a Betrothal (rings, symbolising the promise of faithfulness), consent, marriage prayers with the joining of hands, the crowning, Epistle (Ephesians) and Gospel (Wedding at Cana), a shared cup of wine symbolising the unity of married life, a procession around the table holding the Gospel Book, and removal of the crowns.
facts.conflicts: Melkite is a Lebanese-linked Eastern Catholic church, but this is not a Maronite or Antiochian Orthodox page.

facts.claim: Melkite Eparchy page: citing St John Chrysostom, the crowns symbolise Christ's victory over sin, death and evil; they also symbolise the crown of martyrdom (witness to Christ) and the royal authority of the children of God.
facts.conflicts: Old page's 'king and queen' framing is not supported as worded; nearest sourced idea is 'royal authority of the children of God' (Melkite) and martyrs' crowns (fact_02).

facts.claim: Melkite Eparchy page: under the Canon Law of the Eastern Catholic Churches, the essential elements of the ceremony are the consent, the prayers and blessings of the priest, and the marriage crowns.
facts.conflicts: Maronites are an Eastern Catholic church under the same Code, but no Maronite page was fetched; Maronite crowning stated via this canon-law line only, or [[VERIFY]].

facts.claim: Melkite Eparchy page (history): in the Holy Land in the time of Christ, after the crowning at the bride's father's house the groom led the bride to his house in a procession of his friends and her family, with psalms sung. Historical background, not a description of modern Lebanese practice.
facts.conflicts: No source found for the modern Lebanese departure from the family home; treat as 'often told'.

facts.claim: UNESCO page (HTTP 200, read 3 Nov 2026) is titled 'Al-Zajal, recited or sung poetry', state Lebanon, inscribed in 2014 (9.COM) on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

UNESCO describes Al-Zajal as 'a form of Lebanese folk poetry declaimed or sung at social and family celebrations and in daily life', performed by men and women; poetic jousts with poets and musicians to the rhythm of the tambourine and derbouka. The page does NOT mention weddings by name; it says 'social and family celebrations' and tags 'Family'.
UNESCO says Al-Zajal verses evoke tolerance and dialogue between communities and religions, and that its 'religious and communitarian inclusiveness' promotes its continuity.

Britannica (Islamic arts, Dance and theatre, Arab countries; read 3 Nov 2026): the dabkah is danced mainly by men and is quite common in festivities in the area between northern Syria and southern Israel; the Druze (communities in Lebanon, Syria and Israel) are very fond of it.

Britannica: dabkah performers dance in a straight line holding handkerchiefs high in the air, while the first dancer in the row gives the sign for stepping or jumping. (Britannica does not name the leader 'raas' or 'lawweeh'.)
Britannica dabkah entry, quoting its Lebanon article ('The arts'): Lebanese national folk arts include song, dabkah ('the national dance') and zajal (folk poetry). Spelling as printed: 'dabkah'.

Smartraveller Lebanon: Lebanon recognises dual nationality but treats Lebanese dual nationals as Lebanese citizens, which may limit consular help. Australian Embassy in Beirut: http://www.lebanon.embassy.gov.au/ ; Consular Emergency Centre +61 2 6261 3305 (overseas), 1300 555 135 (in Australia).
Smartraveller Lebanon: celebratory gunfire has caused casualties and often happens during and after political speeches, weddings and funerals.

Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18/08/2026, HTTP 200 on 3 Nov 2026): general advice only; some countries ask you to prove you are free to marry; common documents are a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) or registry certificates; 'We can't tell you what you will need'; contact the destination's embassy or consulate. No fee stated on this page.

Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas': you can't register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if valid where it happened and valid under Australian law had it occurred here; a foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof but may not prove a name change; not recognised if a party is already married, under age, too closely related or forced; talk to a lawyer to confirm validity.

insider_details.detail: Lebanese weddings cross faiths: Britannica lists Shia and Sunni Muslims as the largest groups, Maronites at more than one-fifth, plus other Christians and Druze, so ask each family which pre-wedding steps they actually keep rather than assuming a single Lebanese sequence.

An Orthodox or Eastern Catholic crowning includes a procession three times around the central table with the crowns held behind the couple, so the ceremony space needs a clear central aisle and room around the table; confirm with the officiating priest abroad that the crowning rite can be performed there.

The katb al-kitab can be held at a family home, a mosque, a court or the wedding venue itself, so couples marrying abroad should decide early whether it happens on a separate day or at the venue, and allow a quiet room for the signing with witnesses.

Engagements are usually a family dinner or smaller party with a ring exchange on the right hand, often moved to the left at the wedding, which makes a good intimate pre-wedding event for overseas guests arriving early.
A nice detail for Lebanese Orthodox couples: one crowning prayer asks God to exalt the couple 'like the cedars of Lebanon', which can be printed in the order of service.

A dabke line needs a long clear run of floor, not a small square: Britannica describes a straight line of dancers led by the first in the row, so plan the dance floor (or a terrace) for a line rather than a circle, and confirm floor size with the venue.
Handkerchiefs are part of the dabke as Britannica describes it; a basket of plain handkerchiefs for the line leader and guests is an easy touch at a wedding abroad.

Zajal is a seated, call-and-response form (poets at a table, verses repeated by singers and audience, tambourine and derbouka), so if a family wants recited or sung poetry, schedule it for a quieter dinner moment with amplification, not mid-dance-set. Phrase as advice: UNESCO says 'family celebrations', not weddings.

With Lebanon at 'Do not travel', couples bring these customs to a wedding elsewhere; whatever country they marry in, Smartraveller says to check that country's requirements with its embassy or consulate, and recognition in Australia depends on the marriage being valid there and under Australian law.
